title: 1 Chronicles 11:26–47
context: The list of the mighty men continues name by name, from Asahel the brother of Joab onward. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:24–39 ends with Uriah the Hittite and a total of thirty-seven; Chronicles includes Uriah in 11:41 and then continues with sixteen further names, many of them from east of the Jordan, ending with Jaasiel the Mezobaite. Many names and spellings differ between the two lists, and some names in each list do not appear in the other. These differences are noted rather than resolved. Both traditions read the list as honoring those who served faithfully in David’s rise.

verses.text: The mighty men of the armies also include Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,
verses.arminianNotes: The list begins with Asahel the brother of Joab and Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem. Arminian readers note that Asahel died early in David’s reign (2 Samuel 2:23), so the list honors him after death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see faithful service remembered even after death, as in the 2 Samuel 23:24 notes. Both traditions read the opening names as honoring men who stood with David from the beginning.

verses.text: Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite,
verses.arminianNotes: Shammoth the Harorite and Helez the Pelonite are named. Arminian readers compare 2 Samuel 23:25–26, where the forms are Shammah the Harodite and Helez the Paltite; the variation is left as it stands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samuel also lists Elika the Harodite here, who does not appear in Chronicles. Shared ground: both traditions read the differences as textual issues, while honoring the men named in either list.

verses.text: Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Anathothite,
verses.arminianNotes: Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite and Abiezer the Anathothite are named. Arminian readers note that Tekoa and Anathoth were towns in Judah and Benjamin, showing support for David from several tribes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the list the breadth of loyalty God raised up for David. Both traditions note that these two names match 2 Samuel 23:26–27 closely, unlike many others in the list.

verses.text: Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite,
verses.arminianNotes: Sibbecai the Hushathite and Ilai the Ahohite are named. Arminian readers observe that in the matching slots Samuel reads Mebunnai and Zalmon (2 Samuel 23:27–28), so two of the four names here have no exact counterpart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Sibbecai the Hushathite appears elsewhere as a warrior (2 Samuel 21:18). Shared ground: the name differences between the lists are noted, not harmonized, and both traditions honor the men named.

verses.text: Maharai the Netophathite, Heled the son of Baanah the Netophathite,
verses.arminianNotes: Maharai the Netophathite and Heled son of Baanah the Netophathite are named. Arminian readers note that two men from Netophah, near Bethlehem, appear together, showing local ties within David’s band.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Samuel 23:29 spells the second name Heleb. Both traditions treat the spelling as a minor textual difference and read the verse as honoring two men from the same town.

verses.text: Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the children of Benjamin, Benaiah the Pirathonite,
verses.arminianNotes: Ithai son of Ribai of Gibeah of Benjamin and Benaiah the Pirathonite are named. Arminian readers note that a Benjamite from Gibeah, Saul’s own town, stands among David’s mighty men.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God drawing even men from Saul’s town to David’s side. Shared ground: 2 Samuel 23:29–30 spells the first name Ittai, and both traditions note the difference without resolving it.

verses.text: Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite,
verses.arminianNotes: Hurai of the brooks of Gaash and Abiel the Arbathite are named. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 23:30–31 has Hiddai and Abialbon in the corresponding places, a difference noted rather than resolved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the brooks of Gaash are linked with the hill country of Ephraim (Joshua 24:30), though the exact site is uncertain. Both traditions honor the men named in either form.

verses.text: Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite,
verses.arminianNotes: Azmaveth the Baharumite and Eliahba the Shaalbonite are named. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 23:31 spells the first gentilic Barhumite, a small difference typical of the list.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list’s attention to each man’s town as honoring individuals, not just a group. Shared ground: the second name matches 2 Samuel 23:32, and both traditions read the verse as part of a faithful record.

verses.text: the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite,
verses.arminianNotes: The sons of Hashem the Gizonite and Jonathan son of Shagee the Hararite are named. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 23:32–33 has the sons of Jashen and then Jonathan and Shammah the Hararite.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the relationship between these entries is unclear in both lists. Both traditions name the differences without resolving them and read the verse as honoring those who served with David.

verses.text: Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur,
verses.arminianNotes: Ahiam son of Sacar the Hararite and Eliphal son of Ur are named. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 23:33–34 gives Ahiam’s father as Sharar and has Eliphelet son of Ahasbai in place of Eliphal son of Ur.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see such differences as part of the textual history of the lists, which neither tradition needs to resolve to honor the men. Shared ground: the verse continues the record of David’s warriors.

verses.text: Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite,
verses.arminianNotes: Hepher the Mecherathite and Ahijah the Pelonite are named. Arminian readers note that these names do not clearly correspond to 2 Samuel 23:34, which has Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Eliam is elsewhere named as Bathsheba’s father (2 Samuel 11:3), though Chronicles does not include him here. Both traditions note the difference without speculating about its cause.

verses.text: Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai the son of Ezbai,
verses.arminianNotes: Hezro the Carmelite and Naarai son of Ezbai are named. Hezro is a name the two lists agree on, while his companion appears in Samuel as Paarai the Arbite (2 Samuel 23:35). Arminian readers accept such partial agreement without forcing the names together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Carmel here is likely the town in Judah associated with Nabal (1 Samuel 25:2), though the text does not say so. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the honor roll.

verses.text: Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Hagri,
verses.arminianNotes: Joel the brother of Nathan and Mibhar son of Hagri are named. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 23:36 has Igal son of Nathan of Zobah and Bani the Gadite, a difference in both names and relationships.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the variety of origins among David’s men, some perhaps from outside Israel. Both traditions name the differences and avoid harmonizing, reading the verse as honoring loyal service.

verses.text: Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Berothite (the armor bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah),
verses.arminianNotes: Zelek the Ammonite and Naharai the Berothite, Joab’s armor bearer, are named. Arminian readers note that an Ammonite stands among David’s mighty men, showing that foreigners could serve with honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God gathering people from the nations into the service of his anointed. Shared ground: 2 Samuel 23:37 spells the gentilic Beerothite and speaks of armor bearers, plural; the difference is noted, not resolved.

verses.text: Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,
verses.arminianNotes: Ira the Ithrite and Gareb the Ithrite are named. Arminian readers note that both men share a clan name, perhaps linked to Kiriath Jearim (1 Chronicles 2:53), though the connection is not certain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these two names match 2 Samuel 23:38 exactly. Both traditions read the verse as part of the shared portion of the list, honoring two men of the same clan.

verses.text: Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai,
verses.arminianNotes: Uriah the Hittite and Zabad son of Ahlai are named. Arminian readers note that Uriah’s name recalls David’s grave sin against him (2 Samuel 11), which Chronicles does not narrate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Samuel 23:39 ends the list with Uriah and a total of thirty-seven, while Chronicles continues with Zabad and further names. Shared ground: the difference is noted, and Uriah’s faithful service is honored.

verses.text: Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite (a chief of the Reubenites), and thirty with him,
verses.arminianNotes: Adina son of Shiza, a chief of the Reubenites, is named, with thirty with him. Arminian readers note that this begins the names found only in Chronicles, many from east of the Jordan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Chronicler’s concern to include the eastern tribes in David’s support. Both traditions note that “thirty with him” is unclear, perhaps describing his own band, and avoid pressing its meaning.

verses.text: Hanan the son of Maacah, Joshaphat the Mithnite,
verses.arminianNotes: Hanan son of Maacah and Joshaphat the Mithnite are named. Arminian readers note that little is known of these men beyond this list, yet their service is recorded and remembered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the record of otherwise unknown names a reminder that God notices faithful service. Shared ground: the names are unique to Chronicles, and both traditions read them without speculation.

verses.text: Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hotham the Aroerite,
verses.arminianNotes: Uzzia the Ashterathite, and Shama and Jeiel sons of Hotham the Aroerite, are named. Arminian readers note that the gentilics may point to towns east of the Jordan, though identifications are uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see brothers serving together, a picture of families committed to David’s cause. Both traditions note that Ashtaroth and Aroer are places associated with the eastern regions, without claiming certainty.

verses.text: Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite,
verses.arminianNotes: Jediael son of Shimri and Joha his brother, the Tizite, are named. Arminian readers note another pair of brothers, showing that loyalty to David often ran through whole families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the steady accumulation of names as testimony to God’s provision for David. Shared ground: the gentilic Tizite is otherwise unknown, and both traditions read the verse without guessing its origin.

verses.text: Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite,
verses.arminianNotes: Eliel the Mahavite, Jeribai and Joshaviah sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite are named. Arminian readers note that a Moabite is included, recalling David’s own Moabite ancestry through Ruth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusion of foreigners as part of the Chronicler’s wider picture of those drawn to David. Both traditions read the verse as honoring men from varied backgrounds, while the gentilic Mahavite is uncertain.

verses.text: Eliel, Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliel, Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite close the list. Arminian readers note that the list ends without a total, unlike 2 Samuel 23:39, leaving the record open rather than counted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the long list as the Chronicler’s tribute to the many who helped establish David’s kingdom. Shared ground: the meaning of Mezobaite is uncertain, and both traditions read the list as honoring faithful service.
